L64: # Data type objects (【52†`dtype`】)【53†#】
L65: 
L66: A data type object (an instance of 【52†`numpy.dtype`】 class) describes how the bytes in the fixed-size block of memory corresponding to an array item should be interpreted. It describes the following aspects of the data:
L67: 
L68:   1. Type of the data (integer, float, Python object, etc.)
L69: 
L70:   2. Size of the data (how many bytes is in e.g. the integer)
L71: 
L72:   3. Byte order of the data (【54†little-endian】 or 【55†big-endian】)
L73:   4. If the data type is 【56†structured data type】, an aggregate of other data types, (e.g., describing an array item consisting of an integer and a float),
L74: 
L75:     1. what are the names of the “【57†fields】” of the structure, by which they can be 【58†accessed】,
L76: 
L77:     2. what is the data-type of each 【57†field】, and
L78: 
L79:     3. which part of the memory block each field takes.
L80: 
L81:   5. If the data type is a sub-array, what is its shape and data type.
L82: To describe the type of scalar data, there are several 【59†built-in scalar types】 in NumPy for various precision of integers, floating-point numbers, etc. An item extracted from an array, e.g., by indexing, will be a Python object whose type is the scalar type associated with the data type of the array.
L83: 
L84: Note that the scalar types are not 【52†`dtype`】 objects, even though they can be used in place of one whenever a data type specification is needed in NumPy.
L85: Structured data types are formed by creating a data type whose 【57†field】 contain other data types. Each field has a name by which it can be 【58†accessed】. The parent data type should be of sufficient size to contain all its fields; the parent is nearly always based on the 【60†`void`】 type which allows an arbitrary item size. Structured data types may also contain nested structured sub-array data types in their fields.
L86: Finally, a data type can describe items that are themselves arrays of items of another data type. These sub-arrays must, however, be of a fixed size.
L87: 
L88: If an array is created using a data-type describing a sub-array, the dimensions of the sub-array are appended to the shape of the array when the array is created. Sub-arrays in a field of a structured type behave differently, see 【58†Field access】.
L89: 
L90: Sub-arrays always have a C-contiguous memory layout.
L91: 
L92: Example
L93: A simple data type containing a 32-bit big-endian integer: (see 【61†Specifying and constructing data types】 for details on construction)
L94: 
L95: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L96: 
L97:     >>> import numpy as np
L98: 
L99: 
L100:     >>> dt = np.dtype('>i4')
L101:     >>> dt.byteorder
L102:     '>'
L103:     >>> dt.itemsize
L104:     4
L105:     >>> dt.name
L106:     'int32'
L107:     >>> dt.type is np.int32
L108:     True
L109: 
L110: 
L111: The corresponding array scalar type is 【62†`int32`】.
L112: 
L113: Example
L114: A structured data type containing a 16-character string (in field ‘name’) and a sub-array of two 64-bit floating-point number (in field ‘grades’):
L115: 
L116: > [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L117: >
L118: >     >>> import numpy as np
L119: >
L120: >
L121: >     >>> dt = np.dtype([('name', np.str_, 16), ('grades', np.float64, (2,))])
L122: >     >>> dt['name']
L123: >     dtype('<U16')
L124: >     >>> dt['grades']
L125: >     dtype(('<f8', (2,)))
L126: >
L127: Items of an array of this data type are wrapped in an 【63†array scalar】 type that also has two fields:
L128: 
L129: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L130: 
L131:     >>> import numpy as np
L132: 
L133: 
L134:     >>> x = np.array([('Sarah', (8.0, 7.0)), ('John', (6.0, 7.0))], dtype=dt)
L135:     >>> x[1]
L136:     ('John', [6., 7.])
L137:     >>> x[1]['grades']
L138:     array([6.,  7.])
L139:     >>> type(x[1])
L140:     <class 'numpy.void'>
L141:     >>> type(x[1]['grades'])
L142:     <class 'numpy.ndarray'>
L143: ## Specifying and constructing data types【64†#】
L144: 
L145: Whenever a data-type is required in a NumPy function or method, either a 【52†`dtype`】 object or something that can be converted to one can be supplied. Such conversions are done by the 【52†`dtype`】 constructor:
L146: 
L147: 【52†`dtype`】(dtype[, align, copy])  | --
L148: 
L149: What can be converted to a data-type object is described below:
L150: 
L151: 【52†`dtype`】 object
L152: 
L153: 
L154: Used as-is.
L155: 
L156: None
L157: 
L158: 
L159: The default data type: 【65†`float64`】.
L160: 
L161: Array-scalar types
L162: The 24 built-in 【59†array scalar type objects】 all convert to an associated data-type object. This is true for their sub-classes as well.
L163: 
L164: Note that not all data-type information can be supplied with a type-object: for example, 【66†`flexible`】 data-types have a default itemsize of 0, and require an explicitly given size to be useful.
L165: 
L166: Example
L167: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L168: 
L169:     >>> import numpy as np
L170: 
L171: 
L172:     >>> dt = np.dtype(np.int32)      # 32-bit integer
L173:     >>> dt = np.dtype(np.complex128) # 128-bit complex floating-point number
L174: 
L175: 
L176: Generic types
L177: 
L178: 
L179: The generic hierarchical type objects convert to corresponding type objects according to the associations:
L180: 【67†`number`】, 【68†`inexact`】, 【69†`floating`】  | 【65†`float64`】
L181: 【70†`complexfloating`】  | 【71†`complex128`】
L182: 【72†`integer`】, 【73†`signedinteger`】  | 【74†`int_`】
L183: 【75†`unsignedinteger`】  | 【76†`uint`】
L184: 【77†`generic`】, 【66†`flexible`】  | 【60†`void`】
L185: Deprecated since version 1.19: This conversion of generic scalar types is deprecated. This is because it can be unexpected in a context such as `arr.astype(dtype=np.floating)`, which casts an array of `float32` to an array of `float64`, even though `float32` is a subdtype of `np.floating`.
L186: 
L187: Built-in Python types
L188: 
L189: 
L190: Several Python types are equivalent to a corresponding array scalar when used to generate a 【52†`dtype`】 object:
L191: Python type  | NumPy type
L192: --- | ---
L193: 【78†`int`†docs.python.org】  | 【74†`int_`】
L194: 【79†`bool`】  | 【80†`bool_`】
L195: 【81†`float`†docs.python.org】  | 【65†`float64`】
L196: 【82†`complex`†docs.python.org】  | 【71†`complex128`】
L197: 【83†`bytes`†docs.python.org】  | 【84†`bytes_`】
L198: 【85†`str`†docs.python.org】  | 【86†`str_`】
L199: 【87†`memoryview`†docs.python.org】  | 【60†`void`】
L200: (all others)  | 【88†`object_`】
L201: 
L202: Note that `str_` corresponds to UCS4 encoded unicode strings.
L203: 
L204: Example
L205: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L206: 
L207:     >>> import numpy as np
L208: 
L209: 
L210:     >>> dt = np.dtype(float)   # Python-compatible floating-point number
L211:     >>> dt = np.dtype(int)     # Python-compatible integer
L212:     >>> dt = np.dtype(object)  # Python object
L213: 
L214: 
L215: Note
L216: 
L217: All other types map to `object_` for convenience. Code should expect that such types may map to a specific (new) dtype in the future.
L218: 
L219: Types with `.dtype`
L220: Any type object with a `dtype` attribute: The attribute will be accessed and used directly. The attribute must return something that is convertible into a dtype object.
L221: 
L222: Several kinds of strings can be converted. Recognized strings can be prepended with `'>'` (【55†big-endian】), `'<'` (【54†little-endian】), or `'='` (hardware-native, the default), to specify the byte order.
L223: 
L224: One-character strings
L225: 
L226: 
L227: Each built-in data-type has a character code (the updated Numeric typecodes), that uniquely identifies it.
L228: Example
L229: 
L230: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L231: 
L232:     >>> import numpy as np
L233: 
L234: 
L235:     >>> dt = np.dtype('b')  # byte, native byte order
L236:     >>> dt = np.dtype('>H') # big-endian unsigned short
L237:     >>> dt = np.dtype('<f') # little-endian single-precision float
L238:     >>> dt = np.dtype('d')  # double-precision floating-point number
L239: 
L240: 
L241: Array-protocol type strings (see 【89†The array interface protocol】)
L242: The first character specifies the kind of data and the remaining characters specify the number of bytes per item, except for Unicode, where it is interpreted as the number of characters, and except `b1` which represents boolean. The item size must correspond to an existing type, or an error will be raised. The supported kinds are
L243: `'?'`  | boolean
L244: `'b'`  | (signed) byte
L245: `'B'`  | unsigned byte
L246: `'h'`  | (signed) short
L247: `'H'`  | unsigned short
L248: `'i'`  | (signed) integer
L249: `'I'`  | unsigned integer
L250: `'l'`  | (signed) long integer
L251: `'L'`  | unsigned long integer
L252: `'q'`  | (signed) long long integer
L253: `'Q'`  | unsigned long long integer
L254: `'f'`  | single precision
L255: `'F'`  | complex single precision
L256: `'d'`  | double precision
L257: `'D'`  | complex double precision
L258: `'g'`  | long precision
L259: `'G'`  | complex long double precision
L260: `'O'`  | (Python) objects
L261: `'S'`  | zero-terminated bytes (not recommended)
L262: `'U'`  | Unicode string
L263: `'V'`  | raw data (【60†`void`】)
L264: Example
L265: 
L266: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L267: 
L268:     >>> import numpy as np
L269: 
L270: 
L271:     >>> dt = np.dtype('i4')   # 32-bit signed integer
L272:     >>> dt = np.dtype('f8')   # 64-bit floating-point number
L273:     >>> dt = np.dtype('c16')  # 128-bit complex floating-point number
L274:     >>> dt = np.dtype('S25')  # 25-length zero-terminated bytes
L275:     >>> dt = np.dtype('U25')  # 25-character string
L276: 
L277: 
L278: String with comma-separated fields
L279: A short-hand notation for specifying the format of a structured data type is a comma-separated string of basic formats.
L280: A basic format in this context is an optional shape specifier followed by an array-protocol type string. Parenthesis are required on the shape if it has more than one dimension. NumPy allows a modification on the format in that any string that can uniquely identify the type can be used to specify the data-type in a field. The generated data-type fields are named `'f0'`, `'f1'`, …, `'f<N-1>'` where N (>1) is the number of comma-separated basic formats in the string.
L281: If the optional shape specifier is provided, then the data-type for the corresponding field describes a sub-array.
L282: Example
L283: 
L284: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L285: 
L286:   * field named `f0` containing a 32-bit integer
L287: 
L288:   * field named `f1` containing a 2 x 3 sub-array of 64-bit floating-point numbers
L289: 
L290:   * field named `f2` containing a 32-bit floating-point number
L291: 
L292:     >>> import numpy as np
L293:     >>> dt = np.dtype("i4, (2,3)f8, f4")
L294: 
L295: 
L296:   * field named `f0` containing a 3-character string
L297: 
L298:   * field named `f1` containing a sub-array of shape (3,) containing 64-bit unsigned integers
L299:   * field named `f2` containing a 3 x 4 sub-array containing 10-character strings
L300: 
L301:     >>> import numpy as np
L302:     >>> dt = np.dtype("S3, 3u8, (3,4)S10")
L303: 
L304: 
L305: Type strings
L306: 
L307: 
L308: Any string name of a NumPy dtype, e.g.:
L309: 
L310: Example
L311: 
L312: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L313: 
L314:     >>> import numpy as np
L315: 
L316: 
L317:     >>> dt = np.dtype('uint32')   # 32-bit unsigned integer
L318:     >>> dt = np.dtype('float64')  # 64-bit floating-point number
L319: 
L320: 
L321: `(flexible_dtype, itemsize)`
L322: The first argument must be an object that is converted to a zero-sized flexible data-type object, the second argument is an integer providing the desired itemsize.
L323: 
L324: Example
L325: 
L326: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L327: 
L328:     >>> import numpy as np
L329: 
L330: 
L331:     >>> dt = np.dtype((np.void, 10))  # 10-byte wide data block
L332:     >>> dt = np.dtype(('U', 10))   # 10-character unicode string
L333: 
L334: 
L335: `(fixed_dtype, shape)`
L336: The first argument is any object that can be converted into a fixed-size data-type object. The second argument is the desired shape of this type. If the shape parameter is 1, then the data-type object used to be equivalent to fixed dtype. This behaviour is deprecated since NumPy 1.17 and will raise an error in the future. If shape is a tuple, then the new dtype defines a sub-array of the given shape.
L337: 
L338: Example
L339: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L340: 
L341:     >>> import numpy as np
L342: 
L343: 
L344:     >>> dt = np.dtype((np.int32, (2,2)))          # 2 x 2 integer sub-array
L345:     >>> dt = np.dtype(('i4, (2,3)f8, f4', (2,3))) # 2 x 3 structured sub-array
L346: 
L347: 
L348: `[(field_name, field_dtype, field_shape), ...]`
L349: 
L350: 
L351: obj should be a list of fields where each field is described by a tuple of length 2 or 3. (Equivalent to the `descr` item in the 【90†`__array_interface__`】 attribute.)
L352: The first element, field_name, is the field name (if this is `''` then a standard field name, `'f#'`, is assigned). The field name may also be a 2-tuple of strings where the first string is either a “title” (which may be any string or unicode string) or meta-data for the field which can be any object, and the second string is the “name” which must be a valid Python identifier.
L353: 
L354: The second element, field_dtype, can be anything that can be interpreted as a data-type.
L355: The optional third element field_shape contains the shape if this field represents an array of the data-type in the second element. Note that a 3-tuple with a third argument equal to 1 is equivalent to a 2-tuple.
L356: 
L357: This style does not accept align in the 【52†`dtype`】 constructor as it is assumed that all of the memory is accounted for by the array interface description.
L358: 
L359: Example
L360: 
L361: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L362: Data-type with fields `big` (big-endian 32-bit integer) and `little` (little-endian 32-bit integer):
L363: 
L364:     >>> import numpy as np
L365: 
L366: 
L367:     >>> dt = np.dtype([('big', '>i4'), ('little', '<i4')])
L368: 
L369: 
L370: Data-type with fields `R`, `G`, `B`, `A`, each being an unsigned 8-bit integer:
L371: 
L372:     >>> dt = np.dtype([('R','u1'), ('G','u1'), ('B','u1'), ('A','u1')])
L373: 
L374: 
L375: `{'names': ..., 'formats': ..., 'offsets': ..., 'titles': ..., 'itemsize': ...}`
L376: This style has two required and three optional keys. The names and formats keys are required. Their respective values are equal-length lists with the field names and the field formats. The field names must be strings and the field formats can be any object accepted by 【52†`dtype`】 constructor.
L377: When the optional keys offsets and titles are provided, their values must each be lists of the same length as the names and formats lists. The offsets value is a list of byte offsets (limited to 【91†`ctypes.c_int`†docs.python.org】) for each field, while the titles value is a list of titles for each field (`None` can be used if no title is desired for that field).
L378: The titles can be any object, but when a 【85†`str`†docs.python.org】 object will add another entry to the fields dictionary keyed by the title and referencing the same field tuple which will contain the title as an additional tuple member.
L379: The itemsize key allows the total size of the dtype to be set, and must be an integer large enough so all the fields are within the dtype. If the dtype being constructed is aligned, the itemsize must also be divisible by the struct alignment. Total dtype itemsize is limited to 【91†`ctypes.c_int`†docs.python.org】.
L380: 
L381: Example
L382: 
L383: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L384: Data type with fields `r`, `g`, `b`, `a`, each being an 8-bit unsigned integer:
L385: 
L386:     >>> import numpy as np
L387: 
L388: 
L389:     >>> dt = np.dtype({'names': ['r','g','b','a'],
L390:     ...                'formats': [np.uint8, np.uint8, np.uint8, np.uint8]})
L391: Data type with fields `r` and `b` (with the given titles), both being 8-bit unsigned integers, the first at byte position 0 from the start of the field and the second at position 2:
L392: 
L393:     >>> dt = np.dtype({'names': ['r','b'], 'formats': ['u1', 'u1'],
L394:     ...                'offsets': [0, 2],
L395:     ...                'titles': ['Red pixel', 'Blue pixel']})
L396: 
L397: 
L398: `{'field1': ..., 'field2': ..., ...}`
L399: This usage is discouraged, because it is ambiguous with the other dict-based construction method. If you have a field called ‘names’ and a field called ‘formats’ there will be a conflict.
L400: 
L401: This style allows passing in the 【92†`fields`】 attribute of a data-type object.
L402: 
L403: obj should contain string or unicode keys that refer to `(data-type, offset)` or `(data-type, offset, title)` tuples.
L404: 
L405: Example
L406: 
L407: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L408: Data type containing field `col1` (10-character string at byte position 0), `col2` (32-bit float at byte position 10), and `col3` (integers at byte position 14):
L409: 
L410:     >>> import numpy as np
L411: 
L412: 
L413:     >>> dt = np.dtype({'col1': ('U10', 0), 'col2': (np.float32, 10),
L414:     ...                'col3': (int, 14)})
L415: 
L416: 
L417: `(base_dtype, new_dtype)`
L418: In NumPy 1.7 and later, this form allows base_dtype to be interpreted as a structured dtype. Arrays created with this dtype will have underlying dtype base_dtype but will have fields and flags taken from new_dtype. This is useful for creating custom structured dtypes, as done in 【93†record arrays】.
L419: 
L420: This form also makes it possible to specify struct dtypes with overlapping fields, functioning like the ‘union’ type in C. This usage is discouraged, however, and the union mechanism is preferred.
L421: Both arguments must be convertible to data-type objects with the same total size.
L422: 
L423: Example
L424: 
L425: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L426: 
L427: 32-bit integer, whose first two bytes are interpreted as an integer via field `real`, and the following two bytes via field `imag`.
L428: 
L429:     >>> import numpy as np
L430: 
L431: 
L432:     >>> dt = np.dtype((np.int32,{'real':(np.int16, 0),'imag':(np.int16, 2)}))
L433: 32-bit integer, which is interpreted as consisting of a sub-array of shape `(4,)` containing 8-bit integers:
L434: 
L435:     >>> dt = np.dtype((np.int32, (np.int8, 4)))
L436: 
L437: 
L438: 32-bit integer, containing fields `r`, `g`, `b`, `a` that interpret the 4 bytes in the integer as four unsigned integers:
L439: 
L440:     >>> dt = np.dtype(('i4', [('r','u1'),('g','u1'),('b','u1'),('a','u1')]))
L441: ## Checking the data type【94†#】
L442: 
L443: When checking for a specific data type, use `==` comparison.
L444: 
L445: Example
L446: 
L447: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L448: 
L449:     >>> import numpy as np
L450: 
L451: 
L452:     >>> a = np.array([1, 2], dtype=np.float32)
L453:     >>> a.dtype == np.float32
L454:     True
L455: 
L456: 
L457: As opposed to Python types, a comparison using `is` should not be used.
L458: First, NumPy treats data type specifications (everything that can be passed to the 【52†`dtype`】 constructor) as equivalent to the data type object itself. This equivalence can only be handled through `==`, not through `is`.
L459: 
L460: Example
L461: 
L462: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L463: A 【52†`dtype`】 object is equal to all data type specifications that are equivalent to it.
L464: 
L465:     >>> import numpy as np
L466: 
L467: 
L468:     >>> a = np.array([1, 2], dtype=np.float64)
L469:     >>> a.dtype == np.dtype(np.float64)
L470:     True
L471:     >>> a.dtype == np.float64
L472:     True
L473:     >>> a.dtype == float
L474:     True
L475:     >>> a.dtype == "float64"
L476:     True
L477:     >>> a.dtype == "d"
L478:     True
L479: 
L480: 
L481: Second, there is no guarantee that data type objects are singletons.
L482: 
L483: Example
L484: 
L485: [Button: Try it in your browser!]
L486: Do not use `is` because data type objects may or may not be singletons.
L487: 
L488:     >>> import numpy as np
L489: 
L490: 
L491:     >>> np.dtype(float) is np.dtype(float)
L492:     True
L493:     >>> np.dtype([('a', float)]) is np.dtype([('a', float)])
L494:     False
L495: ## 【52†`dtype`】【95†#】
L496: 
L497: NumPy data type descriptions are instances of the 【52†`dtype`】 class.
L498: ### Attributes【96†#】
L499: 
L500: The type of the data is described by the following 【52†`dtype`】 attributes:
L501: 
L502: 【97†`dtype.type`】  |
L503: 【98†`dtype.kind`】  | A character code (one of 'biufcmMOSTUV') identifying the general kind of data.
L504: 【99†`dtype.char`】  | A unique character code for each of the 21 different built-in types.
L505: 【100†`dtype.num`】  | A unique number for each of the 21 different built-in types.
L506: 【101†`dtype.str`】  | The array-protocol typestring of this data-type object.
L507: Size of the data is in turn described by:
L508: 
L509: 【102†`dtype.name`】  | A bit-width name for this data-type.
L510: 【103†`dtype.itemsize`】  | The element size of this data-type object.
L511: 
L512: Endianness of this data:
L513: 
L514: 【104†`dtype.byteorder`】  | A character indicating the byte-order of this data-type object.
L515: 
L516: Information about sub-data-types in a 【56†structured data type】:
L517: 【92†`dtype.fields`】  | Dictionary of named fields defined for this data type, or `None`.
L518: 【105†`dtype.names`】  | Ordered list of field names, or `None` if there are no fields.
L519: 
L520: For data types that describe sub-arrays:
L521: 
L522: 【106†`dtype.subdtype`】  | Tuple `(item_dtype, shape)` if this 【52†`dtype`】 describes a sub-array, and None otherwise.
L523: 【107†`dtype.shape`】  | Shape tuple of the sub-array if this data type describes a sub-array, and `()` otherwise.
L524: 
L525: Attributes providing additional information:
L526: 【108†`dtype.hasobject`】  | Boolean indicating whether this dtype contains any reference-counted objects in any fields or sub-dtypes.
L527: 【109†`dtype.flags`】  | Bit-flags describing how this data type is to be interpreted.
L528: 【110†`dtype.isbuiltin`】  | Integer indicating how this dtype relates to the built-in dtypes.
L529: 【111†`dtype.isnative`】  | Boolean indicating whether the byte order of this dtype is native to the platform.
L530: 【112†`dtype.descr`】  | __array_interface__ description of the data-type.
L531: 【113†`dtype.alignment`】  | The required alignment (bytes) of this data-type according to the compiler.
L532: 【114†`dtype.base`】  | Returns dtype for the base element of the subarrays, regardless of their dimension or shape.
L533: Metadata attached by the user:
L534: 
L535: 【115†`dtype.metadata`】  | Either `None` or a readonly dictionary of metadata (mappingproxy).
L536: ### Methods【116†#】
L537: 
L538: Data types have the following method for changing the byte order:
L539: 
L540: 【117†`dtype.newbyteorder`】([new_order])  | Return a new dtype with a different byte order.
L541: 
L542: The following methods implement the pickle protocol:
L543: 
L544: 【118†`dtype.__reduce__`】  | Helper for pickle.
L545: 【119†`dtype.__setstate__`】  |
L546: 
L547: Utility method for typing:
L548: 
L549: 【120†`dtype.__class_getitem__`】(item, /)  | Return a parametrized wrapper around the 【52†`dtype`】 type.
L550: 
L551: Comparison operations:
L552: 【121†`dtype.__ge__`】(value, /)  | Return self>=value.
L553: 【122†`dtype.__gt__`】(value, /)  | Return self>value.
